Bogart
BOH-gart
verb (Boomer slang)
From the film star Humphrey Bogart (1899–1957), famous for the cigarette that dangled from his lip and was rarely passed. In late-1960s drug culture to bogart meant to hog a shared marijuana cigarette, from the Fraternity of Man’s song "Don’t Bogart Me" (1968; "Don’t bogart that joint, my friend, pass it over to me"), featured on the Easy Rider soundtrack (1969). The verb broadened to mean to keep something greedily for oneself ("Don’t bogart the popcorn"), and in some regions to bully or muscle in.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To bogart something is to hog it — to keep for yourself what is meant to be shared. The word was born in a drug circle, where a joint was supposed to go around, and the man who held on to it was told not to bogart it. It now applies to anything: the popcorn, the remote, the last slice of pizza. The Christian observation: the setting of the word is not innocent — the believer’s body is "the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1Co 6:19), and the drug circle is no place for it — but the sin the word names is real and common, and Scripture speaks to it directly. Bogarting is selfishness in small things. "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:4). Proverbs describes the economics of generosity: "There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself" (Pro 11:24–25). The Lord Jesus said "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (Act 20:35), and Paul tells the rich to be "ready to distribute, willing to communicate" (1Ti 6:18). A child who learns not to bogart the toys is learning the first lesson of Christian charity; a father who passes the last slice to his son without being asked is teaching it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-1960s drug-culture slang (from Humphrey Bogart’s dangling cigarette; "Don’t Bogart Me," 1968) for hogging what should be shared — a small selfishness Scripture answers: "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (Act 20:35).

BOGART, v.t. (Boomer slang, late 1960s) 1. Originally, to keep a shared marijuana cigarette too long without passing it. 2. To hog; to keep greedily for oneself. "Don’t bogart the chips." 3. (regional) To bully; to force one’s way.

From Humphrey Bogart (1899–1957), the film actor, whose cigarette famously hung from his lip.

Decode for families: the word’s first home was a drug circle. Its common modern meaning is just "hog."

Key Scripture

Php 2:4 — "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others."

Pro 11:24 — "There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty."

Pro 11:25 — "The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself."

Act 20:35 — "I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive."

1Ti 6:18 — "That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;"

1Co 6:19 — "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?"

Modern Corruption

Bogart was born in the drug circle and names hoarding what should be shared; Scripture guards the body as a temple and answers the small selfishness with the blessedness of giving.

expand to see more

The word carries a small irony. In the drug culture, the one sin you could commit was not taking the drug but keeping too much of it. That is a fair picture of how sin works: it creates its own little rules of fairness while breaking God’s. The Christian father need not dwell on the joint; he should simply be honest that the word’s first home was a place his children should not go, and that their bodies belong to the Lord (1Co 6:19).

The sin the word names, though, deserves attention, because it is so ordinary. Most selfishness is not grand; it is the remote, the front seat, the last cookie. Paul’s command in Php 2:4 is the household cure: look also on the things of others. A family that practices passing the plate before taking from it is practicing the gospel in miniature.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Humphrey Bogart (1899–1957) → late-1960s drug slang bogart (hog a joint) → "Don’t Bogart Me" (1968), Easy Rider (1969) → general "to hog."
